report:
**Conclusion: no.** The best evidence indicates that saw palmetto (*Serenoa repens*) preparations do **not** meaningfully improve urinary symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia/enlargement compared with placebo over longer follow-up.

Why this conclusion is well supported:

- An independent, placebo-controlled trial published in 2006 found no difference between saw palmetto and placebo for BPH; the retrieved evidence summary identifies this result directly.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16813360/

- Importantly, later research tested whether the negative result was simply because the usual dose was too low. The evidence summary reports that double and triple doses did not improve lower-urinary-tract symptoms, urinary-flow measures, or prostate size versus placebo.  
  https://archive.connect.h1.co/article/717969419/

- The more recent systematic-review evidence reaches the same conclusion: saw palmetto alone “may result in no clinical benefits” for men with lower-urinary-tract symptoms. Systematic reviews are especially useful here because they assess the totality of randomized-trial evidence rather than one product or trial.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34488251/

- The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health also summarizes the clinical evidence on saw palmetto and BPH.  
  https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/saw-palmetto

This does not mean that individuals cannot feel better while taking it—BPH symptoms can fluctuate and placebo responses occur—but, on average, controlled long-term studies do not show a benefit beyond placebo. Evidence for **mixtures** containing saw palmetto and other herbal products is more uncertain and should not be taken as evidence that saw palmetto itself works.
